# Textual data {#sec-text}

PLAN (Oct 2026)

Keep the book's probabilistic framing throughout: anomalous documents have high surprisal under a language model, or low density in a feature space; authorship verification is a one-class problem (is this text surprising given the author's known work?).

1. From text to numbers (brief)
   - Tokens, document-term matrix, tf-idf, function vs content words, using tidytext (Silge & Robinson, Text Mining with R).

2. Feature-based anomalies in text
   - Document features: length, type-token ratio, word and sentence length, punctuation, sentiment, readability, out-of-vocabulary share.
     Then HDR / stray / LOF on the feature matrix (parallels the ch13 features strategy).
   - Example: wine review descriptions.
     Needs the original `description` column (dropped by fetch_wine_reviews()) restored in the weird package, giving one data set with numerical, categorical and text variables.
     Natural target: reviews whose wording disagrees with their points.

3. Language-model surprisals
   - Unigram / n-gram models give each document a surprisal; perplexity = exp(mean surprisal).
     Show which words drive a document's score.
   - Topic models (LDA) for unusual topic mixtures; document embeddings + PCA (link to ch9).
   - Example: wine review descriptions (same data as section 2).
   - Discussion: detectors of machine-generated text (DetectGPT, Binoculars) flag text that is too predictable, i.e. unusually LOW surprisal.

4. Was this text written by someone else?
   - Stylometric features: frequencies of the most common function words (Mosteller & Wallace).
     Burrows' Delta is a Manhattan distance on standardised frequencies (link to ch6).
   - Authorship verification as one-class anomaly detection: split the author's known works into chunks, model the distribution of their feature vectors, score the questioned text, calibrate by leaving one chunk out.
     Brief mention of unmasking (Koppel & Schler, 2004) and the imposters method.
   - Example: The Royal Book of Oz (1921), credited to L Frank Baum but written by Ruth Plumly Thompson (Binongo, 2003, Chance).
     Gutenberg #30537; Baum's 14 Oz books and several later Thompson Oz books are also on Gutenberg (the latter as a check).

```{r}
#| label: setup11
#| include: false
#| cache: false

source("before-each-chapter.R")
```

Text is an extreme example of categorical data (@sec-categorical-data).
Each word comes from a vocabulary of many thousands of words, most of which are rarely used, and a document is a sequence of words whose meaning depends on their order.
A document is anomalous if it is improbable under a model of the language in which it is written, or if it has features that are very different from other documents in a given corpus.

The chapter starts by converting documents to numbers, and then finds anomalous documents from their features or from their surprisals under a language model.
Then it explores whether a document is surprising given other documents thought to be from the same author; this can help in identifying misattributed authorship.

## From text to numbers {#sec-text-numbers}

Documents cannot be analysed using the methods of @sec-categorical-data, because each contains many words (categorical values), and almost every document is unique.
One relatively simple approach to analysing textual data is to convert each document to a vector of numbers by counting how often each word occurs in it, treating it as a **bag of words** and ignoring the order of the words.
While this loses much of the meaning of the text, it is enough to find many kinds of anomalous documents.

The examples in this section and the next use the tasters' descriptions of the `r scales::comma(NROW(wine_reviews))` wines in the wine reviews data (@sec-data).
They form a large collection of short documents, each describing a wine.
Here are three of them.

```{r}
#| label: fetch-wine-reviews-text
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false

wine_reviews <- fetch_wine_reviews()
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-descriptions
#| code-fold: false
#| class-output: wrap

wine_reviews |>
  slice_head(n = 3) |>
  pull(description)
```

Our task is to find reviews that are anomalous in some way --- substantially different from the other reviews in the data set.

### Tokens and vocabulary

A **token** is a unit of text, and splitting a document into tokens is called **tokenisation**.
Depending on the analysis, the tokens might be single characters, words, pairs of adjacent words, or whole sentences, but in this chapter every token is a single word.
The `unnest_tokens()` function from the **`tidytext`** package\ [@Silge2017] splits text into words by default.
It converts the text to lower case, removes the punctuation, and returns one row for each token, here in a column called `word`.
So we can keep track of which document each token came from, we also add an `id` column to the reviews, which is just the row number of each review in the data frame.

```{r}
#| label: tidytext
#| code-fold: false
#| cache: false

library(tidytext)
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-words
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-descriptions

wine_reviews <- wine_reviews |>
  mutate(id = row_number(), .before = 1)
wine_words <- wine_reviews |>
  select(id, variety, description) |>
  unnest_tokens(word, description, token = "words")
wine_words
vocabulary <- wine_words |>
  count(word, sort = TRUE)
vocabulary
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-words-check
#| include: false
#| dependson: wine-words

top10_share <- sum(vocabulary$n[1:10]) / sum(vocabulary$n)
once_share <- mean(vocabulary$n == 1)
stop_share <- mean(wine_words$word %in% stop_words$word)
# The prose describes the size of the vocabulary and the most common words
stopifnot(
  NROW(wine_words) > 4.5e6,
  between(NROW(vocabulary), 32000, 33000),
  round(100 * once_share) == 38,
  round(100 * top10_share) == 27,
  all(vocabulary$word[1:7] == c("and", "the", "a", "of", "with", "this", "is")),
  vocabulary$word[8] == "wine",
  NROW(stop_words) == 1149,
  round(100 * stop_share) == 44
)
```

The `r scales::comma(NROW(wine_reviews))` descriptions contain `r sprintf("%.1f", NROW(wine_words) / 1e6)` million tokens, but only `r scales::comma(NROW(vocabulary))` distinct words, which together form the **vocabulary**.
A few words are used very often: the ten most common words account for `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * top10_share)`% of the tokens.
At the other extreme, `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * once_share)`% of the vocabulary occurs only once.
This follows the pattern found in almost every large collection of text, known as **Zipf's law**\ [@Zipf1949]: the frequency of a word is roughly inversely proportional to its rank in the list of word frequencies.

Each token is therefore an observation of a categorical variable whose categories are the words of the vocabulary: tens of thousands of categories, most of them rare.
The probability of each word can be estimated from its frequency, as in @sec-categorical, but for most words this estimate rests on only a handful of occurrences, and many possible words don't occur at all.

### Function words and content words

The most common words are "and", "the", "a", "of", "with", "this" and "is".
These are **function words**, which give a sentence its grammatical structure, as distinct from **content words**, such as "wine", "cherry" and "tannins", which carry its meaning.
Lists of function words and other very common words are called **stop words**.

The `stop_words` data in **`tidytext`** combine three overlapping lists, giving `r scales::comma(n_distinct(stop_words$word))` distinct words, and these account for `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * stop_share)`% of the tokens in the descriptions.
Stop words are usually removed when the aim is to find what a document is about, but they are useful words for describing *how* it is written.
Every writer uses these little words in different ways, and their patterns of usage can help identify an author.

Removing them with `anti_join()` leaves the content words.

```{r}
#| label: wine-content-words
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-words

vocabulary |>
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word")
```

### The document-term matrix

The word counts of a collection of $n$ documents form an $n \times m$ **document-term matrix**, with one row for each document and one column for each of the $m$ words in the vocabulary.
The entry in row $i$ and column $w$ is $t_{iw}$, the number of times word $w$ occurs in document $i$.
The sums of each row and column, and the numbers of non-zero entries in each row and column, provide simple summaries of the documents and the words:

- $t_{i\cdot} = \sum_w t_{iw}$, the sum of row $i$, is the number of tokens in document $i$;
- $t_{\cdot w} = \sum_i t_{iw}$, the sum of column $w$, is the number of times word $w$ occurs in the whole collection, which is the frequency used to rank the vocabulary above;
- $m_i$, the number of non-zero entries in row $i$, is the number of distinct words in document $i$, so $m_i \le t_{i\cdot}$ and $m_i \le m$;
- $n_w$, the number of non-zero entries in column $w$, is the number of documents that contain word $w$, called its **document frequency**, so $n_w \le n$.

The total of all the entries, $\sum_i t_{i\cdot} = \sum_w t_{\cdot w}$, is the number of tokens in the collection.
The `cast_sparse()` function builds the matrix from the word counts.

```{r}
#| label: wine-dtm
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-words

dtm <- wine_words |>
  count(id, word) |>
  cast_sparse(id, word, n)
dim(dtm)
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-dtm-check
#| include: false
#| dependson: wine-dtm

dtm_density <- Matrix::nnzero(dtm) / prod(dim(dtm))
stopifnot(
  NROW(dtm) == NROW(wine_reviews),
  NCOL(dtm) == NROW(vocabulary),
  round(100 * dtm_density, 1) == 0.1
)
```

Each description is now a point in a space with $m =$ `r scales::comma(NCOL(dtm))` dimensions, but only `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * dtm_density)`% of the entries are non-zero, so the matrix is stored in a sparse form.
The methods of @sec-highdim could in principle be applied to its rows, but most of the columns are almost entirely zero, and the counts of common words such as "the" contribute far more to any distance between rows than those of rarer words.
So the counts are usually reweighted, or reduced to a few features.

### Term frequency--inverse document frequency

The **term frequency** of word $w$ in document $i$ is the proportion of the document's tokens that are that word, $\text{tf}_{iw} = t_{iw}/t_{i\cdot}$.
The **inverse document frequency** of word $w$ depends on its document frequency $n_w$:
$$
  \text{idf}_w = \log(n / n_w),
$$
which is zero for a word that occurs in every document, and largest for a word that occurs in only one\ [@SparckJones1972].
The product $\text{tf}_{iw} \times \text{idf}_w$, called **tf-idf**, is large for words that are common in document $i$ but rare in the other documents, so it picks out the words that distinguish a document from the rest.
Replacing the counts in the document-term matrix by their tf-idf values gives rare words more weight than common ones, much as MCA gives rare categories more weight (@sec-correspondence).

@fig-wine-tfidf shows the words that are most characteristic of six grape varieties, found by treating all the descriptions of each variety as a single document and computing the tf-idf of each word with `bind_tf_idf()`, using all the varieties in the data as the collection of documents.
The words in the names of the varieties (such as "pinot" and "noir") are removed first, as they are trivially characteristic.

```{r}
#| label: fig-wine-tfidf
#| dependson: wine-words
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   The six words with the largest tf-idf in the descriptions of each of six grape varieties, treating all the descriptions of each variety as a single document.
#| fig-height: 4.5

variety_words <- wine_reviews |>
  distinct(variety) |>
  unnest_tokens(word, variety)
variety_tfidf <- wine_words |>
  filter(!is.na(variety)) |>
  anti_join(variety_words, by = "word") |>
  count(variety, word) |>
  bind_tf_idf(word, variety, n)
varieties <- c(
  "Chardonnay",
  "Pinot Noir",
  "Riesling",
  "Sauvignon Blanc",
  "Syrah",
  "Zinfandel"
)
variety_tfidf |>
  filter(variety %in% varieties) |>
  slice_max(tf_idf, n = 6, by = variety, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tf_idf, y = reorder_within(word, tf_idf, variety))) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(vars(variety), scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_reordered() +
  labs(x = "tf-idf", y = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-tfidf-check
#| include: false
#| dependson: fig-wine-tfidf

top_tfidf <- variety_tfidf |>
  filter(variety %in% varieties) |>
  slice_max(tf_idf, n = 6, by = variety, with_ties = FALSE)
has <- function(v, w) all(w %in% top_tfidf$word[top_tfidf$variety == v])
sweetness <- wine_reviews |>
  filter(variety %in% varieties) |>
  summarise(
    dry = mean(grepl("\\b(dry|sweet)\\b", description, ignore.case = TRUE)),
    .by = variety
  )
# The prose describes the words in fig-wine-tfidf
stopifnot(
  has("Chardonnay", c("oak", "buttered", "pineapple", "toast")),
  has("Pinot Noir", c("cola", "raspberry", "cranberry")),
  has("Riesling", c("lime", "peach", "tangerine", "dry", "off")),
  has("Sauvignon Blanc", c("gooseberry", "grapefruit", "sb")),
  has("Syrah", c("pepper", "meat")),
  has("Zinfandel", c("alcohol", "zin")),
  sweetness$variety[which.max(sweetness$dry)] == "Riesling"
)
```

Most of the words are what a wine drinker would expect: the oak, buttered toast and pineapple of Chardonnay, the cola, raspberry and cranberry of Pinot Noir, the lime, peach and tangerine of Riesling, the gooseberry and grapefruit of Sauvignon Blanc, the pepper and meat of Syrah, and the alcohol of Zinfandel.
The words "dry" and "off" (as in "off-dry") appear for Riesling, whose reviews often say how sweet the wine is, and the tasters' abbreviations "zin" and "sb" survive the removal of the variety names.

## Feature-based anomalies in text {#sec-text-features}

Anomalous documents can be found by describing each document by a few interpretable features, and then applying the multivariate methods of earlier chapters to the features.
The features used here measure the length of a document, its style, its vocabulary and its tone:

- `words`: the number of words;
- `word_length`: the mean number of characters in each word;
- `function_words`: the proportion of the words that are stop words;
- `idf`: the mean of the inverse document frequencies of the words, which is large when a document uses words that are rare in the collection;
- `sentiment`: the number of positive words minus the number of negative words, divided by the number of words, using the list of `r scales::comma(n_distinct(get_sentiments()$word))` positive and negative words compiled by @Hu2004;
- `punctuation`: the number of punctuation marks for each word.

### Reviews with unusual features

We treat each of the `r scales::comma(NROW(wine_reviews))` descriptions as a document and compute the six features for each one.
All but one of the features depend only on the description itself.
The exception is idf, which depends on the whole collection: here $n_w$ is the number of descriptions containing word $w$, not the number of varieties as in @fig-wine-tfidf.

```{r}
#| label: wine-text-features
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-words

idf <- wine_words |>
  distinct(id, word) |>
  count(word) |>
  mutate(idf = log(NROW(wine_reviews) / n)) |>
  select(word, idf)
text_features <- wine_words |>
  left_join(idf, by = "word") |>
  left_join(get_sentiments() |> filter(n() == 1, .by = word), by = "word") |>
  summarise(
    words = n(),
    word_length = mean(nchar(word)),
    function_words = mean(word %in% stop_words$word),
    idf = mean(idf),
    sentiment = (sum(sentiment == "positive", na.rm = TRUE) -
      sum(sentiment == "negative", na.rm = TRUE)) /
      n(),
    .by = id
  ) |>
  left_join(
    wine_reviews |> select(id, points, description),
    by = "id"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    punctuation = stringr::str_count(description, "[[:punct:]]") / words,
    .after = sentiment
  )
text_features
```

Apart from `words`, these features are averages over the words of a review.
The reviews are relatively short, with a median of `r median(text_features$words)` words, so the features will be noisy, especially for the shortest reviews.

The number of words is replaced by its logarithm, the features are converted to robust multivariate $z$-scores with `mvscale()` (@sec-scaling), and a Gaussian mixture model (@sec-gmm-surprisal) is fitted to the scaled features.
Its surprisal probabilities are computed using the GPD approximation of @sec-approximate-surprisal-prob, as the mixture model is unlikely to fit the tails of the distribution well.
With more than 100,000 reviews, fitting the mixture takes several minutes.

```{r}
#| label: mclust-text
#| message: false
#| code-fold: false
#| cache: false

library(mclust)
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-text-gmm-display
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false

Z <- text_features |>
  mutate(words = log(words)) |>
  select(words:punctuation) |>
  mvscale() |>
  as.matrix()
set.seed(1967)
text_gmm <- Mclust(Z, verbose = FALSE) |>
  dist_mclust()
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-text-gmm-fit
#| include: false
#| dependson: wine-text-features

Z <- text_features |>
  mutate(words = log(words)) |>
  select(words:punctuation) |>
  mvscale() |>
  as.matrix()
set.seed(1967)
text_gmm <- Mclust(Z, verbose = FALSE) |>
  dist_mclust() |>
  cache("wine_text_gmm")
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-text-gmm
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-text-gmm-fit

text_features <- text_features |>
  mutate(
    s = surprisals(Z, distribution = text_gmm),
    p = surprisals_prob(Z, distribution = text_gmm, approximation = "gpd"),
    flagged = p < 0.001
  )
text_features |>
  arrange(p) |>
  select(points, words:punctuation, p, flagged)
```

The texts of the twelve least probable reviews are shown below.

```{r}
#| label: wine-text-top
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-text-gmm
#| class-output: wrap

text_features |> slice_min(p, n = 12) |> pull(description)
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-text-check
#| include: false
#| dependson: wine-text-top

flagged_text <- text_features |> filter(flagged)
top_text <- text_features |> arrange(p) |> head(12)
non_review <- grepl("^Imported by|not available", text_features$description)
flagged_non_review <- grepl(
  "^Imported by|not available",
  flagged_text$description
)
short_reviews <- flagged_text |> filter(words <= 10, !flagged_non_review)
percentages <- grepl("%", flagged_text$description)
punct_q99 <- quantile(text_features$punctuation, 0.99)
high_punct <- flagged_text$punctuation > punct_q99
gaultier <- text_features |> filter(grepl("Gaultier", description))
# The prose describes the reviews with the smallest surprisal probabilities
stopifnot(
  NROW(get_sentiments()) == 6786,
  sum(non_review) == 7,
  all(text_features$p[non_review] < 0.001),
  sum(grepl("^Imported by|not available", top_text$description[1:7])) == 6,
  all(top_text$words[1:7] <= 7),
  grepl("^Smells raisiny", top_text$description[7]),
  all(top_text$words <= 12),
  NROW(short_reviews) >= 10,
  median(short_reviews$points) < quantile(text_features$points, 0.05),
  sum(high_punct) >= 20,
  sum(high_punct & flagged_text$words > 10) >= sum(flagged_text$words > 10) / 3,
  sum(percentages) >= 5,
  sum(percentages & high_punct) > sum(percentages) / 2,
  NROW(gaultier) == 1,
  gaultier$p < 0.001,
  between(NROW(flagged_text), 60, 110),
  sum(flagged_text$words <= 10) >= 15,
  all(flagged_text$words < 100),
  sum(flagged_text$words > 10) >= 25
)
```

`r english::Words(NROW(flagged_text))` reviews have surprisal probabilities below 0.001.
Seven of the eight least probable are not reviews at all, but say only that the wine was "Imported by" a named company, or that the review is not available.
The other reviews printed above are very terse, such as "Smells raisiny, feels hot, tastes overripe.", and dismiss the wine in a few words.
The flagged reviews with ten words or fewer have a median of `r median(short_reviews$points)` points, lower than 95% of all reviews.
Many of the longer flagged reviews have much more punctuation than usual: `r english::words(sum(high_punct))` of the flagged reviews have more punctuation marks per word than 99% of all reviews, including most of those that list the percentages of the vineyards or grape varieties in a blend.
Another flagged review is mostly about the packaging rather than the wine: a red vinyl body suit designed for the bottle by the fashion designer Jean-Paul Gaultier.

```{r}
#| label: fig-wine-text-features
#| dependson: wine-text-gmm
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   Number of words and mean inverse document frequency of the wine review descriptions.
#|   The reviews with surprisal probabilities below 0.001, under a Gaussian mixture model of the six text features, are shown in orange.
#| fig-height: 3.5

text_features |>
  ggplot(aes(x = words, y = idf)) +
  geom_jitter(
    data = filter(text_features, p >= 0.001),
    width = 0.01,
    height = 0,
    alpha = 0.05,
    size = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_jitter(
    data = filter(text_features, p < 0.001),
    width = 0.01,
    height = 0,
    colour = "#D55E00",
    size = 1
  ) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Number of words (log scale)", y = "Mean idf")
```

@fig-wine-text-features shows two of the six features.
The descriptions that are not reviews are at the top left, with only a few words, most of them rare.
Many of the other flagged reviews are very short, and the rest are flagged because of their other features, or their combination of features.

### Reviews that disagree with their points

A review can also be anomalous because its text does not fit its other variables.
The points awarded to a wine, on a scale of 80 to 100, should agree with what the taster wrote about it, so a review whose points are surprising given its wording is a **conditional anomaly**, even if neither its points nor its wording is unusual on its own.
As in @sec-mixed, such anomalies are found from the conditional surprisal, $-\log f(\text{points} \mid \text{text})$, here estimated by a linear regression with Normal errors (@sec-regression-log-scores).

The six features above are not much use as predictors, as only the sentiment score measures whether a review is favourable, and it uses a general list of words that knows nothing about wine.
The predictors used instead are the counts of the most common words (those used in at least 500 reviews), along with the logarithm of the number of words.
Each coefficient is then the change in the expected points for each use of that word, holding the other predictors fixed.
The seven descriptions that are not reviews are removed first: an import statement, or a note that the review is not available, says nothing about the wine, so it can neither agree nor disagree with the points.

```{r}
#| label: wine-text-reviews
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-text-gmm

reviews <- text_features |>
  filter(!grepl("^Imported by|not available", description))
```

The regression model has more than 100,000 observations and nearly 1,000 predictors.
To save memory, `model = FALSE` stops `lm()` from storing another copy of the design matrix in its model frame.
Even so, the fitted model is large because it contains the QR decomposition of the design matrix, which `surprisals_prob()` needs for the leverages.
So we keep only the coefficients, fitted values and surprisal probabilities, and then remove the fitted model and the design matrix.

```{r}
#| label: wine-text-points-display
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false

X <- as.matrix(dtm[reviews$id, Matrix::colSums(dtm > 0) >= 500])
fit <- lm(points ~ log(words) + X, data = reviews, model = FALSE)
fit_words <- list(
  coef = coef(fit),
  fitted = fitted(fit),
  p = surprisals_prob(fit, approximation = "gpd")
)
rm(fit, X)
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-text-points-fit
#| include: false
#| dependson: [wine-dtm, wine-text-reviews]

fit_words <- local({
  X <- as.matrix(dtm[reviews$id, Matrix::colSums(dtm > 0) >= 500])
  fit <- lm(points ~ log(words) + X, data = reviews, model = FALSE)
  list(
    coef = coef(fit),
    fitted = fitted(fit),
    p = surprisals_prob(fit, approximation = "gpd")
  )
}) |>
  cache("wine_text_points")
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-text-points
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-text-points-fit

reviews <- reviews |>
  mutate(fitted = fit_words$fitted, p = fit_words$p, flagged = p < 0.001)
coefs <- sort(fit_words$coef[-(1:2)])
names(coefs) <- sub("^X", "", names(coefs))
head(coefs, 10)
tail(coefs, 10)
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-text-points-check
#| include: false
#| dependson: wine-text-points

r2_words <- cor(reviews$points, reviews$fitted)^2
top_pos <- reviews |> filter(points > fitted) |> slice_min(p, n = 6)
top_neg <- reviews |> filter(points < fitted) |> slice_min(p, n = 6)
tonnelles <- top_pos |> filter(grepl("barnyard", description))
top_great <- top_pos |> filter(points >= 96)
# The prose describes the coefficients and the largest residuals in each direction
stopifnot(
  NROW(text_features) - NROW(reviews) == 7,
  length(coefs) == 979,
  round(r2_words, 2) == 0.65,
  all(
    c("lacks", "thin", "flat", "sugary", "short", "simple") %in%
      names(head(coefs, 10))
  ),
  all(
    c("gorgeous", "beautiful", "wonderful", "opulent") %in%
      names(tail(coefs, 10))
  ),
  sum(grepl("^20[0-9][0-9]$", names(tail(coefs, 10)))) == 3,
  between(sum(reviews$flagged), 90, 110),
  sum(top_pos$points >= 96) == 5,
  NROW(tonnelles) == 1,
  tonnelles$points == 92,
  round(tonnelles$fitted) == 83,
  all(sapply(
    c(
      "powerhouse",
      "flat-out dazzling",
      "knockout",
      "almost medicinal intensity",
      "memorable",
      "^95-97"
    ),
    \(x) any(grepl(x, top_great$description))
  )),
  all(abs(top_great$fitted - mean(reviews$points)) < 2.5),
  !any(
    c("powerhouse", "dazzling", "knockout", "memorable", "95", "97") %in%
      names(coefs)
  ),
  all(top_neg$points <= 83),
  all(sapply(
    c(
      "asphalt",
      "Band-Aid",
      "Roquefort",
      "attention for very long",
      "brown around",
      "elegance"
    ),
    \(x) any(grepl(x, top_neg$description))
  )),
  !any(c("barnyard", "asphalt", "band", "roquefort") %in% names(coefs)),
  coefs["flat"] < -1,
  coefs["medicinal"] < -0.5,
  coefs["rustic"] < -0.5,
  coefs["long"] > 0.5,
  coefs["elegance"] > 0.5
)
```

The model explains `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * r2_words)`% of the variation in the points, and doubling the length of a review adds `r sprintf("%.1f", log(2) * fit_words$coef[2])` points to its expected score if the extra words are all rare ones, leaving the counts of the common words unchanged.
The words with the most negative coefficients name faults, such as "lacks", "thin", "flat" and "sugary", or damn with faint praise, such as "simple" and "short".
Those with the most positive coefficients are superlatives, such as "gorgeous", "beautiful" and "wonderful", and years, which occur in advice on when to drink a wine (e.g., "Drink 2023--2035"), given mainly for wines worth keeping.

`r english::Words(sum(reviews$flagged))` reviews have surprisal probabilities below 0.001, `r english::words(sum(reviews$flagged & reviews$points > reviews$fitted))` of them with more points than predicted.
The six least probable reviews in that direction are printed below.

```{r}
#| label: wine-text-points-top
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-text-points
#| class-output: wrap

reviews |>
  filter(points > fitted) |>
  slice_min(p, n = 6) |>
  with(paste(points, "points.", description))
```

Five of these are wines with 96--98 points, but the model predicts only `r round(min(top_great$fitted))`--`r round(max(top_great$fitted))` points for them, close to the average of `r round(mean(reviews$points))` points for all reviews.
Their reviews praise them in words too rare to be among the predictors, such as "powerhouse", "dazzling", "knockout" and "memorable", while some of their common words count against them.
"Flat-out dazzling" contains "flat", whose coefficient is `r sprintf("%.2f", coefs["flat"])`, and "an almost medicinal intensity" contains "medicinal", whose coefficient is `r sprintf("%.2f", coefs["medicinal"])`.
A bag of words gives a word the same weight whatever words surround it.
One review starts with "95-97. Barrel sample.", the taster's range of scores for a wine tasted before it was bottled; the text states the score, but numbers such as these are not among the predictors.

The exception is the third, with `r tonnelles$points` points, whose review is critical: "A rustic wine, with definite barnyard flavors … the tannins and old wood tastes intrude too much."
The model predicts `r round(tonnelles$fitted)` points, and nothing in the text suggests a wine worth 92.
Perhaps the points were recorded against the wrong review; either way, this is the kind of anomaly a conditional model is meant to find.

The six least probable reviews with fewer points than predicted are printed below.

```{r}
#| label: wine-text-points-bottom
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-text-points
#| class-output: wrap

reviews |>
  filter(points < fitted) |>
  slice_min(p, n = 6) |>
  with(paste(points, "points.", description))
```

These are wines with 80--83 points, and their reviews describe the faults in vivid words that are too rare to be among the predictors, such as "asphalt", "Band-Aid" and "Roquefort".
Others use favourable words to unfavourable effect: a wine that "won't hold your attention for very long", and "fading elegance" in a wine that is "brown around the edges".
The coefficients of "long" and "elegance" are `r sprintf("%.2f", coefs["long"])` and `r sprintf("%.2f", coefs["elegance"])`.

The conditional model has found two kinds of anomaly.
A few reviews, such as the third one above, really do disagree with their points.
The others printed above are reviews that a bag of words cannot read: the words that carry their meaning are too rare to be among the predictors, or a common word means something different in context, as in "flat-out dazzling" and "fading elegance".
A model of the language itself can take some of that context into account.

## Language-model surprisals {#sec-text-lm}

A **language model** is a probability distribution for sequences of tokens.
Let $x_{i1}, \dots, x_{iL_i}$ denote the $L_i$ tokens of document $i$.
The probability of the whole document is the product of the probabilities of each token, given the tokens before it, so the surprisal of the document is the sum of the surprisals of its tokens:
$$
  s_i = -\log f(x_{i1}, \dots, x_{iL_i}) = \sum_{j=1}^{L_i} s_{ij},
  \qquad\text{where}\qquad
  s_{ij} = -\log f(x_{ij} \mid x_{i1}, \dots, x_{i,j-1}).
$$
Each token surprisal $s_{ij}$ depends on all the tokens that come before it, which is how a language model takes context into account.
For example, "edges" is not a common word in wine reviews, but after "Looking brown around the" it is almost certain.

The bag of words of @sec-text-numbers corresponds to a language model in which each token is independent of the others, so that $f(x_{ij} \mid x_{i1}, \dots, x_{i,j-1}) = f(x_{ij})$, and context is ignored altogether.
**Large language models** are neural networks that are trained to predict each token from all the tokens before it, using trillions of tokens of text.
They do this far better than any model based on counting words, because they use the meaning of the whole of the preceding text.

### Token surprisals from OLMo 2

The model used here is the smallest version of OLMo 2\ [@OLMo2025], with about a billion parameters.
Unlike most large language models, it has been published along with the data used to train it.
A model that had seen these reviews during training would find them unduly predictable, so it is useful to be able to check whether it did.
A search of the training data\ [@Liu2024] for passages from a sample of about 200 of the reviews found almost none of them.

The tokens of a large language model are not words.
The text is split into pieces from a fixed vocabulary of about 100,000 tokens, so that common words are single tokens (each including the space before it), while rarer words are split into several pieces.
Each review is preceded by the prompt "Wine review:" on a line of its own, so that the model knows what kind of text follows.
Without it, the first few tokens of each review are much more surprising, because the model has no way of knowing that it is reading a wine review.

The model is run from R using the **`reticulate`** package, which calls the Python packages **`torch`** and **`transformers`**.
The first time the code is run, `py_require()` installs these packages (and Python itself if necessary), and `from_pretrained()` downloads the model, which is about 6 GB.
The function `token_surprisals()` computes the surprisal of every token in a batch of reviews.
Reviews of similar length are put in the same batch, as each review in a batch is padded to the length of the longest.
Even so, computing the surprisals for all the reviews took almost five hours on a desktop computer without a graphics processing unit (GPU); with a GPU it is much faster.

```{r}
#| label: wine-olmo-display
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false

library(reticulate)
py_require(c("torch", "transformers"))
torch <- import("torch")
transformers <- import("transformers")
model_name <- "allenai/OLMo-2-0425-1B"
tokenizer <- transformers$AutoTokenizer$from_pretrained(model_name)
olmo <- transformers$AutoModelForCausalLM$from_pretrained(model_name)

# Surprisal of each token in a batch of texts, given the prompt and the tokens before it
token_surprisals <- function(texts, prompt = "Wine review:\n") {
  input <- tokenizer(texts, return_tensors = "pt", padding = TRUE)
  # Start each text with the beginning-of-text token and the prompt
  start <- c(tokenizer$bos_token_id, unlist(tokenizer$encode(prompt)))
  m <- length(start)
  start <- torch$tensor(list(as.list(start)))$expand(length(texts), -1L)
  ids <- torch$cat(list(start, input$input_ids), dim = 1L)
  mask <- torch$cat(list(torch$ones_like(start), input$attention_mask), dim = 1L)
  logits <- with(torch$no_grad(), olmo(ids, attention_mask = mask)$logits)
  # Log probabilities of each token of the texts, from the position before it
  n <- ids$size(1L) - m
  log_probs <- torch$log_softmax(logits$narrow(1L, m - 1L, n), dim = -1L)
  next_ids <- ids$narrow(1L, m, n)
  surprisal <- -log_probs$gather(-1L, next_ids$unsqueeze(-1L))$squeeze(-1L)
  # Transpose so that the tokens of each text are consecutive, dropping padding
  keep <- t(mask$narrow(1L, m, n)$numpy() == 1)
  tibble(
    text = col(keep)[keep],
    token_id = as.integer(t(next_ids$numpy())[keep]),
    surprisal = t(surprisal$numpy())[keep]
  )
}

# Batches of 16 reviews of similar length, to reduce padding
by_length <- wine_reviews$id[order(nchar(wine_reviews$description))]
batches <- split(by_length, ceiling(seq_along(by_length) / 16))
wine_tokens <- lapply(batches, \(b) {
  token_surprisals(wine_reviews$description[b]) |>
    mutate(id = b[text], .before = 1)
}) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  select(-text) |>
  arrange(id)
# Replace the token numbers by the text of the tokens
vocab <- unique(wine_tokens$token_id)
pieces <- vapply(vocab, \(i) tokenizer$decode(list(i)), "")
wine_tokens <- wine_tokens |>
  mutate(token = pieces[match(token_id, vocab)], .after = id) |>
  select(-token_id)
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-olmo
#| include: false
#| dependson: wine-words

wine_tokens <- local({
  library(reticulate)
  py_require(c("torch", "transformers"))
  torch <- import("torch")
  transformers <- import("transformers")
  model_name <- "allenai/OLMo-2-0425-1B"
  tokenizer <- transformers$AutoTokenizer$from_pretrained(model_name)
  olmo <- transformers$AutoModelForCausalLM$from_pretrained(model_name)
  token_surprisals <- function(texts, prompt = "Wine review:\n") {
    input <- tokenizer(texts, return_tensors = "pt", padding = TRUE)
    start <- c(tokenizer$bos_token_id, unlist(tokenizer$encode(prompt)))
    m <- length(start)
    start <- torch$tensor(list(as.list(start)))$expand(length(texts), -1L)
    ids <- torch$cat(list(start, input$input_ids), dim = 1L)
    mask <- torch$cat(list(torch$ones_like(start), input$attention_mask), dim = 1L)
    logits <- with(torch$no_grad(), olmo(ids, attention_mask = mask)$logits)
    n <- ids$size(1L) - m
    log_probs <- torch$log_softmax(logits$narrow(1L, m - 1L, n), dim = -1L)
    next_ids <- ids$narrow(1L, m, n)
    surprisal <- -log_probs$gather(-1L, next_ids$unsqueeze(-1L))$squeeze(-1L)
    keep <- t(mask$narrow(1L, m, n)$numpy() == 1)
    tibble(
      text = col(keep)[keep],
      token_id = as.integer(t(next_ids$numpy())[keep]),
      surprisal = t(surprisal$numpy())[keep]
    )
  }
  by_length <- wine_reviews$id[order(nchar(wine_reviews$description))]
  batches <- split(by_length, ceiling(seq_along(by_length) / 16))
  wine_tokens <- lapply(batches, \(b) {
    token_surprisals(wine_reviews$description[b]) |>
      mutate(id = b[text], .before = 1)
  }) |>
    bind_rows() |>
    select(-text) |>
    arrange(id)
  vocab <- unique(wine_tokens$token_id)
  pieces <- vapply(vocab, \(i) tokenizer$decode(list(i)), "")
  wine_tokens |>
    mutate(token = pieces[match(token_id, vocab)], .after = id) |>
    select(-token_id)
}) |>
  cache("wine_olmo")
```

The result has one row for each token, giving its surprisal in nats.
Here are the first 20 tokens of the first review.

```{r}
#| label: wine-olmo-tokens
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-olmo

wine_tokens |>
  filter(id == 1) |>
  print(n = 20)
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-lm-reviews
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-olmo

lm_reviews <- wine_tokens |>
  summarise(tokens = n(), s = mean(surprisal), .by = id) |>
  left_join(wine_reviews |> select(id, points, description), by = "id")
lm_reviews |>
  arrange(desc(s))
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-lm-check
#| include: false
#| dependson: [wine-lm-reviews, wine-text-gmm]

first_review <- wine_tokens |> filter(id == 1)
tannins <- first_review$surprisal[18:19]
lm_totals <- wine_tokens |> summarise(total = sum(surprisal), n = n(), .by = id)
lm_most <- lm_reviews |> slice_max(s, n = 12)
lm_most_reviews <- lm_most |> filter(!grepl("^Imported by", description))
lm_least <- lm_reviews |> slice_min(s, n = 6)
repeated <- lm_least |> slice_max(tokens, n = 1)
repeated_tokens <- wine_tokens |> filter(id == repeated$id)
half <- nchar(repeated$description) / 2
half_tokens <- floor(NROW(repeated_tokens) / 2)
repeated_s <- c(
  mean(head(repeated_tokens$surprisal, half_tokens)),
  mean(tail(repeated_tokens$surprisal, half_tokens))
)
by_length <- lm_reviews |>
  mutate(short = tokens <= 40) |>
  summarise(m = mean(s), sd = sd(s), .by = short)
feature_flags <- text_features$flagged[match(lm_most_reviews$id, text_features$id)]
least_flags <- text_features$flagged[match(lm_least$id, text_features$id)]
# The prose describes the tokens and the most and least surprising reviews
stopifnot(
  NROW(wine_tokens) == 6258097,
  n_distinct(wine_tokens$id) == NROW(wine_reviews),
  all(trimws(first_review$token[16:19]) == c("Firm", "t", "ann", "ins")),
  all(tannins < 0.06),
  round(cor(lm_totals$total, lm_totals$n), 2) == 0.91,
  round(median(lm_reviews$s), 2) == 3.33,
  round(exp(median(lm_reviews$s))) == 28,
  all(grepl("^Imported by", lm_most$description[1:3])),
  NROW(lm_most_reviews) == 9,
  all(lm_most$tokens < median(lm_reviews$tokens)),
  sum(feature_flags) == 2,
  round(cor(lm_reviews$s, lm_reviews$points), 2) == -0.06,
  by_length$m[by_length$short] > by_length$m[!by_length$short],
  by_length$sd[by_length$short] > by_length$sd[!by_length$short],
  sum(grepl("%", lm_least$description)) == 5,
  !any(least_flags),
  which(lm_least$id == repeated$id) == 4,
  substr(repeated$description, 1, half) ==
    substr(repeated$description, half + 1, 2 * half),
  round(repeated_s, 2) == c(3.31, 0.08)
)
```

"Tannins" is split into three tokens, `" t"`, `"ann"` and `"ins"`.
Once the model has seen `" t"` after "Firm", the rest of the word is almost certain, and the surprisals of "ann" and "ins" are only `r sprintf("%.2f", tannins[1])` and `r sprintf("%.2f", tannins[2])` nats.

### Reviews with surprising wording

The surprisal of a review, the sum of its token surprisals, depends mostly on its length: the correlation between the surprisals of the reviews and their numbers of tokens is `r sprintf("%.2f", cor(lm_totals$total, lm_totals$n))`.
A long review is improbable simply because there are more tokens to predict.
So the reviews are compared using the mean surprisal per token, $\bar{s}_i = s_i / L_i$, computed above.
Its exponential, $e^{\bar{s}_i}$, is called the **perplexity** of the document: the model is as uncertain about each token, on average, as if it were choosing at random from $e^{\bar{s}_i}$ equally likely tokens.
The median review has a mean surprisal of `r sprintf("%.2f", median(lm_reviews$s))` nats per token, or a perplexity of about `r round(exp(median(lm_reviews$s)))`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-wine-lm-length
#| dependson: wine-lm-reviews
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   Number of tokens and mean surprisal per token of the wine review descriptions, under OLMo 2.
#| fig-height: 3.5

lm_reviews |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tokens, y = s)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.01, height = 0, alpha = 0.05, size = 0.3) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Number of tokens (log scale)", y = "Mean surprisal (nats per token)")
```

@fig-wine-lm-length shows that the mean surprisals of short reviews are higher and more variable than those of long reviews.
A short review has fewer tokens to average over, and less context with which to predict each of them.
The texts of the twelve most surprising reviews are shown below.

```{r}
#| label: wine-lm-most
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-lm-reviews
#| class-output: wrap

lm_reviews |> slice_max(s, n = 12) |> pull(description)
```

The three most surprising are import statements, which were also among the least probable descriptions in @sec-text-features.
The other nine are genuine reviews, all of them shorter than the median review, and written in an unusual style: acids that "become jumpy", aromas that are "horsey", a wine that "convinces with simple purity" and another that feels "a bit clampy".
Only two of the nine were flagged by the text features in @sec-text-features.
The mean surprisals are almost unrelated to the points: their correlation is `r sprintf("%.2f", cor(lm_reviews$s, lm_reviews$points))`.
So the language model finds reviews whose wording is unusual, not reviews that disagree with their points.

The six least surprising reviews are shown below.

```{r}
#| label: wine-lm-least
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-lm-reviews
#| class-output: wrap

lm_reviews |> slice_min(s, n = 6) |> pull(description)
```

These are the most formulaic reviews.
Five of them list the percentages of the grape varieties in a blend, and once a review starts with "This blend of 43% Cabernet Sauvignon, 29% Merlot", the names of the other varieties are easy to predict.

The fourth review is different: its text appears twice, the second copy immediately following the first.
@fig-wine-lm-repeat shows its token surprisals.
The mean surprisal of the first half of the tokens is `r sprintf("%.2f", repeated_s[1])` nats, close to the median for all reviews, but that of the second half is only `r sprintf("%.2f", repeated_s[2])` nats: having read the review once, the model predicts it almost perfectly the second time.
None of the six reviews were flagged by the text features in @sec-text-features, and a bag of words cannot detect a repeated text, as repeating a document only doubles its word counts.

```{r}
#| label: fig-wine-lm-repeat
#| dependson: wine-lm-reviews
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   Token surprisals of the review whose text appears twice.
#| fig-height: 3

repeated <- lm_reviews |>
  slice_min(s, n = 6) |>
  slice_max(tokens, n = 1)
wine_tokens |>
  filter(id == repeated$id) |>
  mutate(position = row_number()) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = position, y = surprisal)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Token number", y = "Surprisal (nats)")
```

The repeated review is anomalous because its mean surprisal is unusually *low*: it lies in the lower tail of the distribution of the mean surprisals of the reviews, although the language model finds it highly probable.
Text that has been written by a large language model is also unusually predictable under a similar model, and detectors of machine-generated text are built on this idea\ [@Mitchell2023; @Hans2024].

### Surprising tokens

The token surprisals also show where the surprises are within each review.
The twelve most surprising tokens are shown below, along with the tokens on either side of them.

```{r}
#| label: wine-lm-tokens
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: wine-olmo

wine_tokens |>
  mutate(
    before = paste0(lag(token, 3, ""), lag(token, 2, ""), lag(token, 1, "")),
    after = paste0(lead(token, 1, ""), lead(token, 2, "")),
    .by = id
  ) |>
  slice_max(surprisal, n = 12) |>
  select(id, before, token, after, surprisal)
```

```{r}
#| label: wine-lm-tokens-check
#| include: false
#| dependson: wine-olmo

top_tokens <- wine_tokens |> slice_max(surprisal, n = 12)
top_text <- wine_reviews$description[top_tokens$id]
# The prose describes the most surprising tokens
stopifnot(
  setequal(
    trimws(top_tokens$token),
    c("aket", "otes", "RDD", "nis", "Thin", "fins", "process", "ini",
      "intervention", "negoci", "bowls", "y")
  ),
  all(sapply(
    c("Musaketeller", "tannnis", "finsih", "toprocess", "negociate", "honeysyuckle",
      "Thin Mint", "RDD included", "Case Ibidini", "Pinotesque", "interventionist",
      "bowls it right down the middle"),
    \(x) any(grepl(x, top_text, fixed = TRUE))
  )),
  all(top_tokens$surprisal > 21)
)
```

Six of the twelve are misspellings: "Musaketeller" (for Muskateller), "tannnis", "finsih", "toprocess", "negociate" and "honeysyuckle".
The model has seen countless correctly spelt words, so the surprisal of a misspelt word is concentrated in the token where it departs from the expected spelling.
Three are names or abbreviations that the model could not have expected: "Thin Mint" (a brand of biscuit), "Case Ibidini" (a range of wines) and "RDD" (the taster's abbreviation for Ribera del Duero).
The rest are words or phrases that are unusual in a wine review: "Pinotesque", "interventionist", and a Chardonnay that "bowls it right down the middle" of popular taste.
Each of these tokens has a surprisal above 21 nats, so the model gave it a probability of less than one in a billion.
